title: Expulsion Decreed and Visions of History
setting: Heaven’s throne, then Paradise at dawn and its highest hill, where Michael shows Adam the world to come up to the Flood
summary: The Son presents Adam and Eve’s prayers to the Father, who accepts them but decrees that they must leave Paradise. Michael comes down to deliver the sentence and, while Eve sleeps, shows Adam visions of the future: Cain and Abel, disease, the seduction of the godly, war, and the Flood. Adam learns what his sin has set loose, and also that God will always preserve one just man.

sections.title: The prayers fly up
sections.note: Grace has softened Adam and Eve’s hearts, and their wordless sighs rise to Heaven faster than oratory. Milton compares them to Deucalion and Pyrrha, the pair who prayed to restore mankind after the flood of Greek myth.

sections.title: The Son intercedes
sections.note: The Son, as priest, offers their prayers to the Father as first fruits of grace and asks that their works be grafted onto his own merit. The Father grants everything, but says Paradise can no longer hold them, and death will now be a remedy rather than a curse.

sections.title: Michael is commissioned
sections.note: A trumpet summons the angels, and God announces that Man must be sent out before he eats from the tree of life. He charges Michael to expel the pair without terror, show Adam the future, and set a guard of fire on the east gate.

sections.title: Morning, hope, and ominous signs
sections.note: Adam tells Eve he feels their prayer was heard and hails her as mother of all living; Eve, humbled, hopes they can stay and work content. Then an eagle drives two birds and a lion chases a pair of deer toward the eastern gate, and a bright cloud descends.

sections.title: Michael arrives
sections.note: Michael comes as a warrior prince, solemn rather than friendly like Raphael. Without preface he tells Adam his prayers are heard, but he must leave the garden.

sections.title: Eve’s lament and Adam’s plea
sections.note: Eve mourns the flowers she named and the bower she adorned, and Michael gently tells her that her home is now wherever Adam is. Adam’s deepest grief is losing the places where he talked with God.

sections.title: Michael’s comfort and the hill of vision
sections.note: Michael assures Adam that God is present everywhere, not only in Eden. He puts Eve to sleep, leads Adam up the highest hill, from which all the world’s future empires lie in view, and clears his sight with herbs.

sections.title: Cain and Abel
sections.note: Adam watches a farmer kill a shepherd beside an altar, and Michael explains that these are his sons. Adam realises with horror that he has just seen death.

sections.title: The hospital of diseases
sections.note: Michael shows a ward of every disease, with Death delaying his stroke. He traces such suffering to intemperance and teaches the rule of ‘Not too much,’ which leads to a gentle old age.

sections.title: The tents of pleasure
sections.note: Adam is charmed by a scene of music, metalwork and lovely women, until Michael explains that these are Cain’s descendants, who will seduce the godly ‘sons of God.’ Adam blames woman; Michael blames man’s weakness.

sections.title: The giants’ wars and Enoch
sections.note: Adam sees cities at war and giants glorying in slaughter. One just man who speaks of right is snatched away in a cloud: Enoch, taken by God because he dared to be just.

sections.title: Noah and the Flood
sections.note: Peace turns to luxury, and one reverend man preaches in vain, builds an ark and takes in the animals. The Flood drowns everything else, and the narrator turns to Adam, drowned in his own flood of tears.

sections.title: Michael explains the Flood
sections.note: Michael shows how conquest breeds corruption in victors and vanquished alike, until only Noah is just. He adds that the Flood will tear the mount of Paradise loose and leave it a bare salt island, since God gives no holiness to a place.

sections.title: The waters recede; the rainbow
sections.note: The flood shrinks, the ark grounds on a mountain, and the dove returns with an olive leaf. Adam rejoices, and Michael explains the rainbow as God’s covenant never again to destroy the earth by water.

glosses.note: Grace that comes before any human effort and makes repentance possible.

famous.why: Eve’s farewell to her flowers is one of the tenderest speeches in the poem.
Death shaking his dart over the sick but delaying to strike, though they beg for him: a grim emblem of suffering.
The image of a good death as ripe fruit dropping into its mother’s lap.
‘Nor love thy life, nor hate; but what thou livest live well’: Michael’s whole moral teaching in two lines.
Fame goes to conquerors, ‘and what most merits fame, in silence hid,’ a recurring Miltonic conviction.

themes: Grace comes first: repentance is God’s gift working in the fallen.
The Fall’s consequences unfold through history as violence, disease, lust and war.
Holiness belongs to people and their obedience, not to places.
In every corrupt age God preserves one just man who stands against the crowd.
art: Michael and Adam on the summit of Paradise’s highest hill, the angel pointing down to the ark riding the flood beneath a rainbow.
